{"text":"# Working on a RectSL study

## The wall

A RectSL program is a finite animated scene made of rectangles:

- `->wall 16 9 meters` sets the wall. Every frame shows the whole wall and nothing outside it. The
  wall's centre is `(0, 0)`, `+x` is right and **`+y` is up**, so a 16 × 9 wall runs from x -8 to 8
  and y -4.5 to 4.5. `->xy` places a rectangle's centre; `->wh` and `->square` are full widths.
- `->duration 6` is the clip's length in seconds; the window plays it and loops. Time outside the
  keys of a track holds the nearest key. `->fps` is how finely the clip is sampled for analysis and export.
- **Colours are sRGB, as typed.** `0x808080` is mid grey in the window and in every tool image;
  `rgb 0.5 0.5 0.5` is the same grey. `->background 0x101014` colours the wall behind everything.
- Rotation is in radians (`tau` is a full turn). Later rectangles draw over earlier ones; `->layer`
  and `->front`/`->back` change that.

The scene box is a child of a RectSL root, usually the window box. Once run, the window draws the
scene live and follows every edit that compiles, so a person's typing and a model's accepted edit
both appear there. The tools draw their evidence the same way on the same window's GPU, and say so
in `renderedBy`; with no window they use a CPU reference that draws the same geometry at one sample
per pixel. The study card in the scene box's output shows the clip as a filmstrip, holds the window
at a time, and has a slider for every number that previews in the window as it moves.

## Idioms that hold

```rectsl
"sun" rect  3 2 ->xy  1.5 ->square  0xffcc33 solid ->fill ;       # a named rectangle
"bar" rect  '( 0=-6  3=6  6=-6 ) ->x ;                             # a quote in a channel is a track: t=value keys
"blink" rect  1 ->square  '( 0=0  1=1 ) ease-in-out 2 loop-time ->alpha ;   # shape a track, then loop it every 2 s
"pip" rect 0.4 ->square  12 3 '( f0 tau * ->rot ) radial ;         # 12 copies round a circle of radius 3
"cell" rect 0.8 ->square  9 '( fc 6 * 0 ->xy  "viridis" f colormap solid ->fill ) array ;   # one colour per copy
"dot" rect 0.5 ->square  '( 0=-4  2=4 ) ->y  8 '( fc 7 * ->x  i 0.25 * ->delay-all-time ) array ;   # one motion, each copy later
```

- **Name what you make** (`"sun" rect`). Names are what a person reads, what `TraceRectSLStudy`
  reports, and what `CompareRectSLStudy` matches across revisions; an unnamed rectangle's id
  (`rect-12`) moves when a line above it adds one.
- **Reproduce, then vary:** `array`, `radial`, `grid`, `arc`, `spiral` and `sunflower` copy one
  template; inside the body `i`, `f` (0..1), `f0` (0..1, cyclic), `fc` (-1..1), `ic`, and in a grid
  `colc`/`rowc` vary each copy. `->delay-all-time` and `->stagger-time` give copies a canon in time.
- **A seamless loop** ends where it starts: give the last key the first key's value at
  `->duration`, or `loop-time` with a period that divides the duration.
- **Share motion** with a named track: `linear-track "rise" '( 0=-3 6=3 )` once, then
  `"rise" track-ref ->y` in every rectangle that should move together.
- **Colour per copy** comes from the stack through `colormap` (`"magma" f colormap solid ->fill`) or
  from opacity (`f 0.8 * 0.2 + ->alpha`); a two-colour ramp across a rectangle is `linear`.
- **Materials are StackSL** fragment programs over `vec4(uv of the rectangle, object id, seconds)`,
  multiplied by the rectangle's colour: `material stripes '( uv 8 * sin abs )`, then
  `stripes ->material`. Geometry belongs in RectSL, shading in the material.

## Traps

- **`rgb`, `rgba`, `material`, `track`, `->wall`, `->duration`, `->fps` read literals forward** out of
  the source, not off the stack: `rgb 0.9 0.4 0.2`, never `0.9 0.4 0.2 rgb`, and no expression can
  go in those slots. For a computed colour use `colormap`.
- **A clone's `->xy` replaces both x and y**, including a y track it inherited. To keep the
  template's y motion on its copies, set only `->x`.
- **Give a material to each copy as it is made**, inside the `array` body; applying one afterwards
  through `descendants … each` has been seen to reach only some rectangles.
- **Rectangles are mostly outside the wall** is the usual reason for a blank frame: check the wall's
  extent and `TraceRectSLStudy`. The check warns when nothing is visible at its probe times, and
  about rectangles that are never visible or leave early.
- **`{{ … }}` Kotlin escapes** compile Kotlin the first time they are seen (about a tenth of a
  second each); prefer RectSL words and `colormap` when they will do.

## Tools

| Tool | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `RectSLStudyGuide` | This guide, or the words guide searched for a word. |
| `InspectRectSLStudy` | Checked source, live edit state, history, the scene's shape, warnings, lines, knobs. Once per turn. |
| `EditRectSLStudy` | Whole program. First draft or rewrite. |
| `PatchRectSLStudy` | Exact unique replacements to the live source. |
| `SetRectSLNumbers` | New values for knobs by index; a hex colour takes its 24-bit number. |
| `ObserveRectSLStudy` | Frames at chosen times, measurements, optional comparison with another revision. |
| `TimelineRectSLStudy` | The whole clip as frames, plus what is visible and moving over time and the events in it. |
| `TraceRectSLStudy` | `identify`: every rectangle outlined and labelled with its line; `build`: the scene after each line. |
| `KnobsRectSLStudy` | Knobs, what reads each, and how much a 10% nudge to each changes the frames. |
| `SweepRectSLNumber` | One knob at 2..9 values, unpublished. |
| `TryRectSLVariants` | 1..8 candidates drawn side by side and held for adoption, unpublished. |
| `AdoptRectSLVariant` | Publish a held candidate. |
| `RestoreRectSLRevision` | Make an old revision current again, as a new revision. |
| `CompareRectSLStudy` | What an edit preserved: pixels outside a region, and which rectangles changed, by line. |
| `ExportRectSLStudy` | A PNG frame or an MP4 of the clip into the document's files. |

Every edit is a transaction. It names the revision you read and the hash of the live source you
read; if the person has typed since, it is refused and nothing is overwritten — Inspect again and
build on their edit. A candidate that does not compile, or whose materials do not, is refused with
the problem and its line, and the box keeps the checked scene. The person sees and edits the same
program: its problems appear on its lines as they type, and when they run the box it is checked in
as a revision like any of yours.

## Evidence and its limits

Frames are drawn at pixel centres, so a rectangle thinner than a pixel at the size asked for can
vanish from a frame without vanishing from the scene: ask for a larger `size`, or read `Trace`'s
numbers. Visible counts and events come from the scene itself, not the pixels: a rectangle is
visible when it is not transparent and meets the wall, even if another covers it. A still frame
says nothing about motion; use `TimelineRectSLStudy` or several times when the request is about
how something moves or when.

## Style

Write scenes a person can read and change:

```rectsl
# asked: three moons crossing a violet sky, slowly
# chosen: 12 s clip; each moon a named rect on its own named track, so they can be moved separately
->wall 16 9 meters
->duration 12
->fps 30
0x1a1030 ->background

# the moons, left to right, each rising a little later
linear-track "cross" '( 0=-9  12=9 )
"moon-a" rect  0 1.5 ->xy  1.2 ->square  0xf4efe0 solid ->fill  "cross" track-ref ->x ;
...
```

The header's `(asked)` lines record what the person said, the `(chosen)` lines what you decided for
them. One object per paragraph, each with a comment saying what it is. When a later request
overrides an earlier one, edit the header to say so.
"}

{"text":"[Model] RectSL is a small stack language with scene side effects. Numbers, strings, colors, quotes, selections, rects, groups, paints, and scalar tracks can sit on the stack. Most geometry words apply to the active rect/group or to the current selection.
[Objects and groups] A scene is a tree of named rects and groups, and the names are how you get back to anything after you have moved on. Below: a group `orbit` holding two squares — one authored, one a `clone` of it shifted along +x, both tagged `petal`. Then the whole group is deep-copied into a `twin` three units lower, and finally every `petal` anywhere in the scene (four of them now, two per copy) is gathered out of its existing parent into a new group `petals`.
[Objects and groups] "orbit" group
[Objects and groups] all rects  '( "petal" tagged? ) filter  "petals" ->group-selected ;
[Objects and groups] | `group` | `[id] -- group` | Opens a group scope. New objects become group children until `end` / `end-group`. |
[Objects and groups] | `end`, `end-group` | `--` | Closes the current group. |
[Objects and groups] | `->select` | `id -- object` | Selects a rect or group and pushes its reference. |
[Objects and groups] | `group?` | `-- bool` | `1` when the active object is a group. |
[Objects and groups] | `copy-deep`, `clone-deep` | `-- object` | Deep copy of a group and its descendants. |
[Objects and groups] | `->group-selected` | `selection [id] -- group` | Reparents selected objects into a new group. |
[Selection and transforms] | `all` | `-- selection` | Selects every scene node. Follow with `rects`, `groups` or a predicate to narrow the selection. |
[Selection and transforms] | `roots` | `-- selection` | Selects only top-level scene nodes. Children remain reachable through their groups. |
[Selection and transforms] | `children` | `selection -- selection` | Replaces a group selection with its direct children. Use `descendants` when deeper nested objects should also be included. |
[Selection and transforms] | `descendants` | `selection -- selection` | Selects every descendant of the selected groups. Unlike `children`, it traverses the nested hierarchy. |
[Selection and transforms] | `rects`, `groups` | `selection -- selection` | Filters the selection to rectangles or, with `groups`, to groups. Other node types are removed from the selection. |
[a centered grid whose cell alpha ripples with distance from the middle] | `array` | `[template] count quote -- selection` | Reproduce a template object `count` times, running `quote` on each copy with array context. Element 0 is the template itself; the rest are fresh clones (deep for groups). Template is the active object, or a rect/group taken from the stack. Pushes the selection of all copies. |
[Data visualization] Dense data is an explicit target for RectSL. A **colormap** turns a value in `[0, 1]` into a perceptually-uniform colour; a **`Data`** value is a plain numeric list you can normalize and bind to size/colour; the **chart words** fold both into ready-made bar charts, heatmaps, and scatter plots. All three emit ordinary rects: `each`, `->stagger-time`, `group` and tracks all still apply to the result."}

{"text":"[Geometry and ordering] | `->rot`, `->rotation` | `scalar --` | Sets rotation in radians. A track animates the angle over time. |
[Geometry and ordering] | `->alpha` | `scalar --` | Sets the opacity channel. Supply a track to fade the object over time. |
[Geometry and ordering] | `->live` | `birth life --` | Emitter primitive: play the object's animation from `birth` (local time 0 = `birth`) and show it only during `[birth, birth+life]`. |
[Tracks] Track quotes are flat `time value` pairs. An optional `=` may sit between the time and value of a key to read the pairing aloud: `0=0.2` means "0.2 at time 0". The two forms are interchangeable and may be mixed:
[Track transforms] A track is a value, so it can be bent before it is assigned. All five rects below ride the *same* three-key sweep from x=-8 to x=+8; only the time axis differs. `delayed` starts a second and a half late, `slower` spaces its keys 1.4× farther apart, `bounced` plays forward then backward over a two-second period, and `eased` shapes the interpolation with a Penner curve and then loops it. Stacked in rows, one motion falls into a round — which is the cheapest way to see what a retiming word actually did.
[Track transforms] "delayed" rect  0  1 ->xy  1 ->square  '( 0=-8  2=0  4=8 ) 1.5 delay-time ->x ;
[Track transforms] "slower"  rect  0 -1 ->xy  1 ->square  '( 0=-8  2=0  4=8 ) 1.4 time* ->x ;
[Track transforms] "bounced" rect  0 -3 ->xy  1 ->square  '( 0=-8  1=8  2=-8 ) 2 pingpong-time ->x ;
[Track transforms] "eased"   rect  0 -5 ->xy  1 ->square  '( 0=-8  2=8 ) ease-in-out 2 loop-time ->x ;
[Track transforms] | `delay-time` | `track seconds -- track` | Moves every key later by the supplied number of seconds. The value curve is preserved. |
[Track transforms] | `scale-time` | `track factor -- track` | Multiplies key times by a factor. A factor above one makes the same motion occupy more time. |
[Track transforms] | `reverse-time` | `track -- track` | Reverses the track’s key times. Use it to traverse an existing motion backwards. |
[Track transforms] | `loop-time` | `track period -- track` | Repeats a track over the supplied period in seconds. The original track remains the motion sampled within each period. |
[Track transforms] | `pingpong-time` | `track period -- track` | Alternates forward and backward traversal of the track. Use it to avoid an abrupt jump from the end back to the start. |
[Track transforms] | `time+` | `track seconds -- track` | Shifts the track’s key times by a number of seconds. It is the compact form of a time offset. |
[Track transforms] | `time*` | `track factor -- track` | Scales the track’s key times by a factor. Use it to retime the same key values. |
[Track transforms] | `snap-time` | `track grid -- track` | Snaps key times to the supplied time grid. This quantizes timing rather than key values. |
[Track transforms] | `keys-before` | `track time -- track` | Keeps the keys at or before the supplied time. Use it to select an early portion of a track. |
[Track transforms] | `keys-after` | `track time -- track` | Keeps the keys at or after the supplied time. Use it to discard an earlier part of a track. |
[Track transforms] | `keys-between` | `track start end -- track` | Keeps keys in the supplied start/end window. The arguments are times rather than key indices. |
[Selection and transforms] Build first, then sort the scene out by logic. `pip` is one spinning square tagged `spark`, reproduced nine times by `array` — each copy's opacity set from its centred fraction, so the row is brightest at the ends — and then spread 1.4 units apart by `->stagger`. The next four lines never name an individual rect again: a mirrored clone is folded across the axis x=3 and pushed to the front of its layer; every rect in the scene is dimmed a further 10%; every object *tagged* `spark` is scaled up; and the original's whole timeline is made to loop every two seconds.
[Selection and transforms] "pip" ->select  2 ->loop-all-time ;
[Selection and transforms] | `->delay-all-time` | `seconds --` | Shifts all tracks on the object or selection later by the supplied seconds. Their relative timing stays together. |
[Selection and transforms] | `->scale-all-time` | `factor --` | Multiplies every key time by the supplied factor. Values above one spread keys farther apart in time. |
[Selection and transforms] | `->reverse-all-time` | `--` | Reverses every track across the scene duration. This keeps the object’s channels synchronized while reversing the motion. |
[Selection and transforms] | `->loop-all-time` | `period --` | Repeats all tracks with the supplied period. The period is in seconds. |
[Selection and transforms] | `->pingpong-all-time` | `period --` | Alternates forward and backward playback of all tracks. The supplied period controls the repeated time mapping. |
[Selection and transforms] | `->stagger-time` | `stepSeconds --` | Adds increasing delays in selection order. The step is measured in seconds per object. |
[Loops and blocks] Three loops, three shapes of the same idea. `times` runs its body eight times with the index in `i`, so the first row is eight cells spread 2.2 units apart — and their opacity comes out of a *predicate* rather than a curve: cells 2 through 6 are dimmed, the rest bright, written with comparisons and `not`. `range` counts over an explicit interval. `repeat` does the same but reaches for `loop-count` to normalise its index into `[0, 1]` first, which is how a loop places things by fraction rather than by step.
[Loops and blocks] ) times
[Loops and blocks] | `times` | `count quote --` | Runs quote `count` times and pushes the index before each run. |
[Loops and blocks] | `repeat` | `count quote --` | Runs quote `count` times. Use `i`, `n`, or `loop-count` inside. |
[Array primitives] Array primitives *reproduce a subexpression with modification*: the Fischinger idea of one shape multiplied into a rhythm of copies, each shifted in space, time, size, or colour. Inside any `repeat`/`range`/`array`/`grid`/`radial` body the per-copy context words below are available; combine them with `mix`, `->offset`, `->rotate`, `->polar`, and `->delay-all-time` to vary each copy.
[a centered grid whose cell alpha ripples with distance from the middle] | `array` | `[template] count quote -- selection` | Reproduce a template object `count` times, running `quote` on each copy with array context. Element 0 is the template itself; the rest are fresh clones (deep for groups). Template is the active object, or a rect/group taken from the stack. Pushes the selection of all copies. |
[a centered grid whose cell alpha ripples with distance from the middle] | `grid` | `cols rows quote -- selection` | Runs `quote` `cols·rows` times to build fresh cells, with grid context available. Close each cell with `;` like `repeat`. Pushes the selection of created objects. |
[a centered grid whose cell alpha ripples with distance from the middle] | `->split` | `[template] count t quote -- selection` | At time `t` the template vanishes and `count` shards are born at its split-point position (sampled from its tracks). Each shard's flight is authored by `quote` around the origin in split-relative local time (array context available), then placed at the split point. Pushes the shard selection. |
[Data visualization] Dense data is an explicit target for RectSL. A **colormap** turns a value in `[0, 1]` into a perceptually-uniform colour; a **`Data`** value is a plain numeric list you can normalize and bind to size/colour; the **chart words** fold both into ready-made bar charts, heatmaps, and scatter plots. All three emit ordinary rects: `each`, `->stagger-time`, `group` and tracks all still apply to the result.
[a bar chart from literal data, staggered fade-in, coloured by value] 0.08 ->stagger-time
[Data] | `data` | `quote -- data` | Run `quote` and collect every `Number` it leaves into a `Data` list (`'( 3 1 4 1 5 ) data`, or computed: `'( 8 times [ i i * ] ) data`). |
[Musicality — the pattern language as scene structure] RectSL's array primitives distribute copies in *space*. The musical layer distributes them in *time*, by borrowing [Field's Tidal-inspired pattern language](pattern_language.md) whole. The two fit together because they are already the same shape. A RectSL track is `sample(t)`; a pattern is `events(arc)`. Both are pure functions of time, with no simulation state. So a pattern **is** a track, and a pattern event, which carries an onset and a real duration, **is** a `->live` window."}

[Colormaps] | `colormap`, `cmap` | `name t -- color` | Look up a named ramp at `t` in `[0, 1]` (clamped). Pushes a `Color` usable anywhere colour is (`solid`, `linear`, `->fill`, `rgb`). Names: `viridis`, `magma`, `inferno`, `plasma`, `turbo`, `coolwarm` (diverging), `grayscale`. |
[one template, sixteen strikes: four a bar, each alive for its own quarter] '( 0=0  0.10=1  0.5=0 ) linear ->alpha
[Variation on a selection] "echo" rect  0.6 ->square  '( 0=-8  4=8 ) linear ->x  0.4 ->y
[Distribution curves (Functions bridge)] Linear `mix` is rarely the shape you want across an array. RectSL borrows [`afield.stdlib.Functions`](functions_examples.md), a tested library of easings, distributions and noise defined over `[0, 1]`. That is exactly the range of the array fraction `f`. `ease` shapes a scalar/track through the full Penner family; the curve words push a reusable `Fn` value you `sample` at `f` (or any x). The curves are graph-backed, so the Functions rewrite/evolve tooling can optimise an array's distribution toward a target.
[`reflect` mirrors a curve about 0.5; `tile` repeats it k times across the array] | `ease` | `->x name -- ->x` / `track name -- track` | Shape a value through a named Penner easing. `name` is any of `linear`, `quad-in/out/in-out`, `cubic-…`, `quart-…`, `quint-…`, `sine-…`, `expo-…`, `circ-…`, `back-…`, `elastic-…`, `bounce-…`, `smoothstep`, `smootherstep`. A constant eases to a number; a keyed track eases its interpolation. |
[Stack and scalar operators] One `grid`, and every number in it computed rather than typed. Each cell knows its own centred column and row, so `colc dup * rowc dup * + sqrt` is its distance out from the middle — and from that one quantity the cell derives its opacity (a smoothstepped falloff, floored at 0.05 and clamped), its size (a power curve of the same distance, so cells shrink outward non-linearly), and its rotation (the two axes averaged, then quantised to quarter-turns of π, so the field reads as banded rather than smooth).
[Stack and scalar operators] | `mix`, `lerp` | `a b t -- out` | Linearly interpolates between a and b by t. Zero selects a and one selects b. |"}
